issues.legal_issue: Territorial application of tenancy legislation does not deny equality solely because it applies to only part of a state.
material_facts: The challenged rent-settlement scheme applied to the former territory of Marwar and not to every area of the larger state.
The respondents stated that rents and cesses in the relevant tenancy area had been higher than those in other areas and that earlier local laws had addressed those differences.
The petitioners neither alleged nor proved that conditions in the other areas were similar to those in the area covered by the scheme; the other areas also had their own rent laws.
issues.conclusion: The scheme did not violate Article 14 merely because it applied to only part of the state; the petitioners had not established that persons in the differently treated areas were similarly situated.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits unequal treatment of persons similarly situated. Territorial classification is permissible when germane to the enactment's purpose, and tenancy legislation is not invalid merely because it does not cover an entire state. The Court referred to Bowman v. Lewis, and applied the principles in Biswambhar Singh v. The State of Orissa and Thakur Amar Singhji v. State of Rajasthan.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_regional_ten: A party challenged the constitutionality of a tenancy law that applies to only part of a larger state.
predicates.local_tenancy_conditions_differ: The tenancy conditions in the covered area differed from conditions in areas outside the law's coverage.
predicates.comparable_conditions_not_proved: The challenger did not establish that conditions in the covered and uncovered areas were similar.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a tenancy law limited to one region and local conditions differ or comparable conditions are not proved, the regional application does not violate equality.

issues.legal_issue: Conducting rent settlements in different areas at different times does not deny equality merely because the resulting rent rates may differ.
material_facts: The scheme based rent rates on averages from the ten years preceding settlement.
Settlement operations could be undertaken only by specialised staff with technical knowledge and administrative experience.
The state could not necessarily conduct settlement operations throughout the entire covered area at the same time, so different areas could be settled on different dates and produce different rates.
issues.conclusion: The possibility that settlements conducted at different times would produce different rent rates did not make the scheme discriminatory under Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not prohibit differences arising from settlement operations conducted at different times where simultaneous operations across the whole area are impracticable. The Court applied Biswambhar Singh v. The State of Orissa and Thakur Amar Singhji v. State of Rajasthan, which upheld provisions permitting action in different areas on different dates.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_phased_rent_: A party challenged the constitutionality of a rent-settlement scheme under which different areas may be settled at different times.
predicates.specialised_settlement_capacity_is_limit: Settlement work requires specialised staff and the state cannot necessarily undertake it across the whole area simultaneously.
predicates.settlement_timing_may_affect_rates: The settlement method could result in different rates because the areas are assessed at different times.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns phased rent settlement, limited specialised capacity and the possibility of rates varying with settlement timing do not prevent the settlement from proceeding without violating equality.

issues.legal_issue: A scheme fixing fair and equitable rent for tenanted land does not infringe a landlord's property right merely by limiting the rent that may be recovered.
material_facts: The scheme required rent to be fixed as fair and equitable rent for cultivating tenants.
In fixing rent, the settlement authority considered prior collections and other agricultural factors, while excluding years declared abnormal.
An abnormal year could involve either unusually high or unusually low yields, so excluding such years could benefit either landlords or tenants.
issues.conclusion: The scheme did not violate Article 19(1)(f), because a landlord's property right in tenanted land extended only to receiving reasonable rent, and the provision excluding abnormal years was not unfair or unreasonable.
issues.legal_principle: For a landlord whose land is cultivated by a tenant, the right to hold and enjoy the property includes the right to receive reasonable rent. Legislation intended to fix fair and equitable rent does not invade that right. Excluding abnormal years from an average is not inherently unreasonable where abnormality may involve either unusually high or unusually low yields. The relevant provisions were sections 81 to 85 of the Marwar Land Revenue Act, including section 82.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tenancy_rent: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law regulating rent payable by cultivating tenants.
predicates.scheme_aims_at_reasonable_rent: The law's purpose is to fix fair and equitable rent rather than to deprive the landlord of property.
predicates.rent_assessment_accounts_for_abnormal_yi: The rent assessment excludes abnormal years, including years of unusually high or low yield, when calculating the relevant average.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a tenancy rent scheme aimed at reasonable rent and its assessment accounts for abnormal yields, the regulation does not infringe the landlord's property right.

issues.legal_issue: Giving a reasonable rent rate retrospective effect does not infringe a landlord's property right to hold land.
material_facts: The scheme authorised the settlement authority to make a rent rate payable from a date earlier than the date on which the rate was fixed.
The challenged provision was part of a scheme for fixing fair and equitable rent.
The petitioners did not challenge the merits of the particular order giving the rate an earlier effective date; they challenged the provision as part of their attack on the scheme.
issues.conclusion: Retrospective operation of a reasonable rent rate did not violate Article 19(1)(f); consequently, it was unnecessary to decide whether the provision qualified as a regulatory restriction under Article 19(5).
issues.legal_principle: A landlord's right to hold property in tenanted land is a right to recover reasonable rent. If the rent fixed is reasonable for the period after settlement, the Court considered it reasonable for the preceding period as well. In the absence of an infringement of Article 19(1)(f), no question arises under Article 19(5). The Court considered section 86 of the Marwar Land Revenue Act.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_retroactive_: A party challenged a law allowing a rent rate for tenanted land to take effect from an earlier date.
predicates.rate_is_reasonable: The rent rate fixed under the scheme is reasonable.
predicates.scheme_regulates_rent_for_tenanted_land: The law regulates the rent payable by a tenant for land held by a landlord.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns retrospective tenancy rent, a reasonable rate under a scheme regulating rent for tenanted land does not infringe the landlord's property right.

issues.legal_issue: A law regulating the landlord-tenant relationship does not constitute compulsory acquisition merely because it reduces the landlord's rent rights.
material_facts: The rent-settlement scheme could reduce the rent payable to a landlord, including by giving the settled rate effect from an earlier date.
The scheme regulated the relationship between landlords and cultivating tenants; it did not acquire the land for the state.
issues.conclusion: The scheme did not violate Article 31(2), because regulating the landlord-tenant relationship and diminishing a landlord's rights did not amount to taking property.
issues.legal_principle: A law regulating the relationship between landlord and tenant is not a taking of property within Article 31(2), even if it reduces the landlord's rights. The Court relied on Thakur Jagannath Baksh Singh v. United Provinces, including the Federal Court and Privy Council decisions concerning the distinction between regulation of landlord-tenant rights and compulsory acquisition.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tenancy_rent: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law regulating rent between landlords and tenants.
predicates.law_changes_landlord_tenant_rent_rights: The law reduces or otherwise changes rights held by a landlord in relation to rent payable by a tenant.
predicates.land_is_not_compulsorily_acquired: The law regulates the tenancy relationship without compulsorily acquiring the land.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns tenancy rent regulation that changes landlord-tenant rent rights without compulsory acquisition of the land, the regulation is not compulsory acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A reasoned power to set an earlier effective date for rent rates is not arbitrary merely because it leaves broad discretion to the settlement authority.
material_facts: The law permitted the settlement authority to make a rent rate effective from an earlier date only if it thought fit to do so for reasons.
The law did not specify all circumstances in which an earlier date could be chosen.
Although civil courts could not examine the order's reasonableness, the Board of Revenue had revisional jurisdiction over settlement orders.
The petitioners relied on a prior case involving a power exercisable on an authority's subjective satisfaction, where the decision was final and could not be questioned in civil courts.
issues.conclusion: The power to select an earlier effective date was reasonable and valid; it did not confer absolute and uncontrolled discretion or encroach on the landlord's property right.
issues.legal_principle: Wide discretion is not necessarily arbitrary, particularly where the authority must give reasons for exercising it and a higher revenue authority has revisional jurisdiction. The Court distinguished Thakur Baghubir Singh v. Court of Wards, Ajmer, where the power depended on subjective satisfaction and the decision was final and not open to challenge in civil courts. The relevant provisions were sections 62, 86 and 233 of the Marwar Land Revenue Act.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_settlem: A party challenged the constitutionality of discretion given to an authority administering rent settlement.
predicates.earlier_effective_date_requires_reasons: The authority may choose an earlier effective date only for stated reasons.
predicates.revenue_revision_is_available: A higher revenue authority has revisional jurisdiction over the settlement order.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns rent-settlement discretion, a reasoned choice of an earlier effective date subject to revenue revision is not arbitrary.
